component.name: Apache Ranger
component.description: Framework to enable, monitor and manage comprehensive data security across 20+ data processing services. A central web application (Ranger Admin) authors fine-grained authorization policies; lightweight per-service Java plugins, deployed inside each data service's own process, pull those policies and enforce authorization decisions locally. In threat-model terms Ranger is a distributed Policy Decision / Policy Enforcement system, complemented by a user/group sync daemon, an optional tag-sync daemon, a PDP server exposing a network authorization API, an audit framework, and Ranger KMS for HDFS transparent encryption. The threat model is v1.1, reviewed by the Ranger PMC on 2026-06-12.

externalReferences.comment: Source security model document; this file is a structured translation of it.

blueprints.name: Ranger distributed PDP/PEP deployment
blueprints.description: Multi-component distributed system deployed across a cluster: Ranger Admin (default port 6080), usersync/tagsync daemons, the PDP server, the audit framework, Ranger KMS, and a fleet of plugins each embedded inside a separate data-service process on trusted intra-cluster hosts. End users of guarded data services never talk to Ranger directly; their identity and requested action are the inputs to the embedded plugin (PEP).

assets.name: Ranger Admin
assets.description: Central web application and REST API (/service/..., /public/v2/api/...) where administrators author policies, manage users/roles, and view audits. Highest-value component: anyone who can author policy can grant access to all guarded data.

assets.name: Per-service plugins (PEPs)
assets.description: Java plugins running inside each guarded data service's process (HDFS NameNode, HiveServer2, HBase server, Kafka, NiFi, Trino, ...). They pull policy from the Admin at a configured interval (e.g. 30 seconds), cache the last-known policy, evaluate (principal, resource, action) requests locally, and emit audit records. Fully trusted once authenticated, a deliberate design choice.

assets.name: PDP service
assets.description: Separate process exposing a network authorization API (/authz/*) for callers that cannot embed a PEP. Requires an authenticated client (Kerberos/JWT/trusted-header); only liveness/readiness/metrics probes are reachable unauthenticated.

assets.name: Usersync and tagsync daemons
assets.description: Usersync reads user/group data from LDAP/AD/Unix and writes it to the Admin DB; tagsync feeds classification tags from Atlas/Kafka. Policy integrity is only as good as these feeds.

assets.name: Ranger KMS
assets.description: Key management service for HDFS transparent encryption; keys live in a DB or HSM. Modeled at its own trust level because it handles key material.

assets.name: Audit framework
assets.description: Records allow/deny decisions and administrative actions to configured sinks (Solr/OpenSearch, HDFS, RDBMS, Kafka, log file). Audit is a record, not a control.

assets.name: Policy, user, and audit stores
assets.description: Relational database backing the Admin policy/audit/user store, plus audit sinks and the KMS key store. Ranger assumes these stores are access-controlled and integrity-preserving.

zones.name: End users of guarded data services
zones.description: Principals whose HDFS/Hive/etc. access Ranger authorizes. Untrusted with respect to the decisions Ranger makes about them; they are authenticated by the host service, not by Ranger.

zones.name: Guarded data-service hosts
zones.description: Trusted, administered cluster nodes running the data services with embedded Ranger plugins.

zones.name: Ranger central services
zones.description: Ranger Admin, PDP service, usersync/tagsync, and the audit framework.

zones.name: Administrative clients
zones.description: Security administrators (trusted for the instance), delegated administrators (trusted for their delegated scope only), auditors (read-only), and key admins (KMS only) using the Admin UI or REST API.

zones.name: Identity and tag sources
zones.description: LDAP/AD/Unix identity stores read by usersync and Atlas/Kafka tag feeds read by tagsync; trusted as the authority for user/group membership and tags.

zones.name: Backing stores
zones.description: Relational database, audit sinks (Solr/HDFS/...), and the KMS key store (DB/HSM); assumed access-controlled and integrity-preserving.

zones.name: Key management
zones.description: Ranger KMS and its key material; a distinct trust level within the deployment.

boundaries.name: Internal data plane (sync sources and backing stores)

persona.description: Authors policies, manages users/roles, views audits via the Admin UI or REST API. Trusted for the instance; the model does not defend against a malicious top-level administrator.
A group owner to whom administration of a subset of resources has been delegated. Trusted for their delegated scope only; overreach by a delegated admin is in scope.
May view policies and access audits but not author them; writes are blocked.

roles.name: End user of a guarded data service

persona.description: The principal whose data access Ranger authorizes. Untrusted; authenticated by the host service, not by Ranger, and never interacts with Ranger directly.

assumptions.description: JVM-based runtime with modern JDK module assumptions; components are deployed within a cluster network where plugin nodes are administered hosts, not internet-facing machines.

An external authentication authority (typically Kerberos, plus LDAP/AD for user/group identity) establishes principal identity before authorization is requested; Ranger trusts the identity the PEP presents.
The backing relational database, audit sinks, and KMS key store are themselves access-controlled and integrity-preserving.

TLS is recommended in production, but plaintext HTTP is the shipped and supported default (maintainer-confirmed); a report that reduces to traffic being unencrypted by default is by-design operator hardening, not a vulnerability.

When Ranger is the ACL enforcer and no policy matches, the result is deny, except the HDFS service, which falls through to the host's native ACLs. If a plugin can neither evaluate fresh nor cached policy it denies (again except HDFS fallthrough).
Time-bound policies assume reasonably synchronized clocks across Admin and plugin nodes; the policy-evaluation engine is thread-safe under concurrent reads and periodic policy refresh.

Ranger seeds bootstrap accounts (admin, rangerusersync, rangertagsync, keyadmin), but the installer mandates an explicit, complexity-checked password on fresh install; a seeded/default password is not a supported production posture.

threats.name: Authorization decision diverges from authored policy
threats.description: An end user of a guarded data service gains access the policy denies (or is denied access the policy grants) by manipulating the requested resource/action or exploiting policy-evaluation edge cases (resource-name matching, wildcard/recursion handling, case sensitivity, tag-vs-resource precedence). An existing deny-policy (or the absence of any grant) that nonetheless yields access is CVE-class VALID per the PMC.

threats.name: Policy interception or substitution on the plugin-to-Admin channel
threats.description: A network peer impersonates the Admin to a plugin (or a plugin to the Admin), or intercepts/substitutes policy in transit. The policy-download path is authenticated (Kerberos, JWT, or header-based auth with a trusted proxy), but plaintext HTTP is the shipped default, so policy substitution or MITM on an unprotected channel is an attack class left to the operator.

threats.name: Unauthenticated or under-privileged administrative action
threats.description: An unauthenticated actor or an under-privileged/delegated administrator authors or reads policy outside their scope, escalates their own role, or reads audits/keys they should not. Administrative actions must be access-controlled; a low-privilege or delegated administrator exceeding their delegated scope is an in-scope adversary.

threats.name: Audit record tampering or forgery by a non-admin
threats.description: A non-admin able to tamper with or forge audit records is a security finding (maintainer-confirmed). Missed records alone are correctness-grade. Audit-store injection (e.g. log/Solr injection via crafted resource names) is a related attack class left to the integrator/operator.

threats.name: Unauthorized key retrieval from Ranger KMS
threats.description: A KMS client obtains key material for keys it is not authorized to use. The key is the KMS-policy resource; unauthorized key retrieval is CVE-class VALID per the PMC.

threats.name: Hang inside the host service on crafted resource input
threats.description: A hang or CPU exhaustion inside the host service caused by crafted resource input to the policy engine may be a security issue. Super-linear evaluation cost in policy size or resource-string length is NOT a bug (maintainer-confirmed); whether Ranger makes no resource guarantee at all was deferred by the PMC for later ratification.

threats.name: Forged identity or tag data injected upstream of Ranger
threats.description: A malicious identity/tag source, or someone able to inject into usersync/tagsync inputs, forges group/role membership or classification tags and thereby gains policy grants. Policy is only as trustworthy as the identity/tag source; upstream injection is out of model (the identity source is trusted), so securing the directory and tag-source channels is the operator's responsibility.

threats.name: Stale policy enforced during the revocation-propagation window
threats.description: Plugins cache the last-known policy and pull changes at a configured interval, so a just-revoked grant may persist until the next successful pull. The revocation-propagation delay is by design (maintainer-confirmed); cached policy is availability, not authority, and operators must not treat revocation as instantaneous.

threats.name: Policy and audit exposure on plaintext transport
threats.description: Plaintext HTTP is the shipped and supported default for plugin-to-Admin and UI-to-Admin traffic; plaintext deployment exposes policy and audit in transit. Ranger supports TLS but does not enforce it at the protocol layer, so a report that reduces to traffic being unencrypted by default is by-design operator hardening, not a code vulnerability.

threats.name: Compromised or Byzantine plugin host
threats.description: An attacker with code execution on a node running a plugin has already defeated the PEP locally; Ranger cannot defend a PEP against its own compromised host. Every PEP is fully trusted once authenticated, a deliberate design choice that keeps runtime overhead low, and Ranger makes no cross-node integrity claim. Out of scope.

threats.name: Forged or spoofed end-user principal
threats.description: Ranger authorizes an already-authenticated principal and does not establish identity. A forged principal accepted by the host service's authentication layer is the host service's or cluster Kerberos's problem, not Ranger's. Out of scope.

threats.name: Malicious top-level security administrator
threats.description: The fully-trusted security administrator is the root of authority for the Ranger instance; the model does not defend the guarded data against a malicious omnipotent admin. Delegated admins overreaching IS in scope. Out of scope, together with side-channel and co-tenancy adversaries (maintainer-confirmed out of scope).

threats.name: Direct compromise of the database, audit store, or key store
threats.description: Compromise of the backing database, audit store, or key store directly (bypassing Ranger) is that store's own trust boundary and out of scope; the operator must secure these stores independently.

threats.name: Guarded-service access path that does not consult the plugin
threats.description: A Ranger deny is not a sandbox: enforcement depends on the host service actually calling the plugin for every access path. A code path in the guarded service that does not consult the plugin is not protected by Ranger, and resource-name canonicalization mismatches between the host service and the policy engine are a shared responsibility with the host service (maintainer-confirmed), not a Ranger-only defect.

trustBoundaries.name: End user access request boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Primary untrusted-input boundary: the requested resource name and action are derived from an untrusted user, though the identity is asserted by the host service's authentication layer, which Ranger trusts.

trustBoundaries.name: Policy distribution boundary
trustBoundaries.description: The plugin trusts that downloaded policy genuinely originates from the legitimate Admin server, and the Admin trusts that only authorized plugins download policy. Authenticated via Kerberos, JWT, or header-based auth with a trusted proxy; the local policy cache is load-bearing.

trustBoundaries.name: Administration boundary
trustBoundaries.description: The highest-value boundary: anyone who can author policy can grant themselves or others access to all guarded data. REST endpoints fall into three buckets: public (login/static, health, metrics), plugin/PEP identity (policy/tag/role download and grant/revoke), and authenticated admin/user (everything else, with session plus @PreAuthorize RBAC and writes blocked for the read-only Auditor).

trustBoundaries.name: Internal data plane boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Usersync/tagsync feeds and the Admin's database, audit sinks, and key store: integrity of the user/group/role data and the policy store determines the integrity of every downstream decision. Identity and tag sources are trusted as authoritative; the stores are trusted infrastructure.

trustBoundaries.name: KMS key operation boundary
trustBoundaries.description: Ranger KMS releases key material only to clients authorized by key-access policy; key operations are performed by authenticated KMS clients.

controls.name: Bounded, thread-safe policy evaluation with fail-safe default
controls.description: The policy-evaluation engine is bounded and thread-safe (maintainer-confirmed). When Ranger is the ACL enforcer and no policy matches, the result is deny, except HDFS, which falls through to native ACLs; if a plugin can neither evaluate fresh nor cached policy it denies (except HDFS fallthrough).

controls.name: Authenticated policy download and authorization API
controls.description: Plugins and the PDP service authenticate via Kerberos, JWT, or header-based auth with a trusted proxy to download policy; the PDP's /authz/* API requires an authenticated client and the server refuses to start with no auth handler configured. Secure download variants additionally require a user in policy.download.auth.users.

controls.name: Admin authentication and role-based access control
controls.description: The Admin authenticates management/UI users via LDAP, AD, Unix, PAM, Kerberos/SPNEGO, Knox SSO, header, JWT, or internal DB, and enforces session plus @PreAuthorize RBAC on REST endpoints, with writes blocked for the read-only Auditor role and delegated admins confined to their delegated scope. The installer mandates an explicit, complexity-checked admin password on fresh install.

controls.name: Centralized audit of access and administrative actions
controls.description: Allow/deny decisions and administrative actions are recorded to the configured audit sink (Solr/HDFS/DB/log). Disabling audit voids the auditability property; audit is a record, not a control, and absence of an audit record is not proof access was blocked.

controls.name: KMS key-access policy authorization
controls.description: Ranger KMS authorizes each key operation against key-access policy and releases key material only to authorized clients.

controls.name: Enable and require TLS with mutual authentication
controls.description: Enable and require TLS on UI-to-Admin and plugin-to-Admin channels, with mutual authentication so a plugin cannot be impersonated and policy cannot be intercepted or substituted. TLS is recommended in production but plaintext HTTP is the shipped default.

controls.name: Restrict network exposure of Ranger endpoints
controls.description: Deploy plugins only on trusted, administered cluster nodes inside the trust boundary; never expose the Admin REST API or the policy-download endpoint to untrusted networks. Anyone reaching policy-write endpoints can grant themselves access to all guarded data.

controls.name: Secure and authenticate identity and tag sources
controls.description: Secure and authenticate the LDAP/AD/Unix directory connection used by usersync and the Atlas/Kafka channel used by tagsync, and verify the upstream Kerberos authentication layer so the principal identities Ranger authorizes are genuine. Tag-based policy is only as trustworthy as the tag feed.

controls.name: Secure the backing database, audit sinks, and key store
controls.description: Secure the backing DB, audit sinks (Solr/HDFS), and the KMS key store independently; Ranger trusts them. Do not disable audit and then rely on it for compliance evidence.

controls.name: Size the policy-pull interval to data sensitivity
controls.description: Understand that revocation propagates only at the policy-pull interval (plus cache); size that interval to the sensitivity of the guarded data and do not assume instant revocation.
